subsubtopic: AMENDMENT DELINEATING GOVERNMENT'S POWER IN DISPOSING OF PUBLIC LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who just spoke is one of the few members of parliament who has been privileged to travel to a location in Canada that is very vitally concerned with a large portion of this bill, 8,500 square miles, to put it in precise
National Parks Act
terms. It will probably be the largest national park to be established in Canada in the Kluane region of the Yukon.
Many members do not appreciate the fact of all the members of this chamber, the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth) and I come here in a triple capacity. This is because the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) is responsible for our municipal wellbeing. He is responsible for our territorial wellbeing in the sense that term is used in a provincial way. Of course, we are also here representing our constituents on the federal level. Having that responsibility under the terms of the Yukon Act and the Northwest Territories Act, two federal statutes which set up these two separate territorial jurisdictions, whatever the minister does very vitally effects every level of government in both territories. Indeed, he is responsible and has the power to affect every level of government in both territories.
One of the themes I have been following since coming into this chamber is that the federal government has been remiss, and has sadly neglected, the two northern territories with respect to the establishment of national parks in those jurisdictions. I have also been saying repeatedly that the federal government should not simply embark on a frolic of its own, to unilaterally and arbitrarily carve out areas in these territories, without having any consultative process with the elected representatives of the people in the two territories. If the minister were here, he would say there has been this kind of process adopted in so far as the Yukon is concerned. I gainsay him on that. I do not believe that process has been followed.
One of the things I welcome is the fact we are now debating a stage in this bill which will result in it going to the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development for consideration by that committee which is scheduled to travel to the Yukon Territory on December 10 for the whole week. While there, that committee will hold public meetings, three if necessary. One will be at Whitehorse, one at Dawson City, which was classified as an area of national historic interest, and a third at Haines Junction which will be the hub of the national park proposed to be set up by this statute.
Let me comment here that I am continually amazed by the utter gall of this government. They say they want parliament to approve a national park in the Yukon, a national park in the Northwest Territories in the Nahanni area and on Baffin Island. However, for the past two years the government has been spending the taxpayers' dollars from the consolidated revenue fund for the purpose of proceeding with the development of all these parks, certainly the one in the Yukon, without approval by parliament of the bill now before us. We are, in effect, being asked to rubber stamp something the government has already committed millions of dollars to develop. It amuses me when I see in the bill provisions with respect to consultation. For example, the provision in clause 2 of the bill stipulates, and I quote:
The Governor in Council may, by proclamation, amend the schedule by adding to any park described therein lands described in the proclamation where the Governor in Council is satisfied that

November 26, 1973
National Parks Act
(b) agreement has been reached with the province in which the lands are situated that the lands are suitable for addition to a National Park;
The government's idea of consultation is that it should make a unilateral decision and, having made that decision, go to the other government concerned and ask: What are your views? Sotto voce, they say: We do not really care, because we have made up our minds, but we must go through the process of consultation. It is the same when it comes to the so-called consultative process involving the Indian people. I wonder how many of the organizations the government funded so that they might be set up for the purpose of dialogue have been consulted concerning the establishment of national parks at Kluane, at Nahanni, or on Baffin Island. I should say precious little. They make up their minds and, having done so, they disclose their plans. Then, they hear views which they call input, but these views do not change their decision one iota.
There is a still more serious objection which we take in the Yukon and in the Northwest Territories, if I may presume to speak for my colleague in the New Democratic Party. In the north, in the two territories, all lands, for the most part, are owned by the government over which this House of Commons purports to exercise a measure of control. Clause two stipulates that the government may add land to any park provided it can reach an agreement with the province in which the land is situated. Now, according to the Interpretation Act, a statute of this parliament, a province is defined as including both territories. One would, therefore, assume that the same kind of agreement must be reached with each of the territorial governments as must be reached with the provinces before any extension of park boundaries can come about.
But it is the minister himself who is the government of the Yukon and of the Northwest Territories. So, when it comes to the implementation of this clause he puts on his hat as federal Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and says to the Yukon or the Northwest Territories: I am obliged by this legislation to secure your agreement, since certain lands are situated within the boundaries of your jurisdiction, that it is in order to extend the boundaries of a national park. Then, he takes off his hat as federal minister and puts on his hat as minister responsible for the government of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories and says to himself: I agree with you that the boundaries should be extended. That is the situation, and shows how ridiculous this kind of provision for consultation is as far as the Yukon and the Northwest Territories are concerned.
The fact of the matter is that what the minister decides determines what will take place in those two northern territories. If he wants to extend the boundaries of the Kluane National Park from roughly 8,500 square miles to 207,031 square miles, indeed, the whole of the area of the Yukon Territory, and make it a people reserve, he can do just that. I am not arguing against the notion of a people reserve. Sometimes, when I have spent too long in these southern areas of Canada I think it would be a good idea to set up a people reserve, such as the Yukon is at the moment. But I do object to legislation such as this, supposedly intended to work throughout Canada for the bene-

fit of all Canadians, being designed to cover only provincial requirements without regard for any meaningful consultation or any-if I might use a phrase which seems, now, to have been discarded-any provision for participatory democracy being contained in it whatsoever.
Throughout the debate on whether or not federal parks should be established in the north, I have maintained that what the government should be doing, particularly when the acquisition of such a vast area of land and such a vast amount of potentially resource-rich reserve is under consideration, is first of all to make a careful assessment of the commercial and resource potential of that land before unilaterally and arbitrarily establishing the area as a park. I do not think this is being done. I do not think I am being unfair to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) and his predecessors or to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and his predecessors, when I charge them with failing to act in accordance with this very reasonable and logical approach. No real assessment has been made of the potential. The consequence is that in the Yukon, at any rate-I am not as familiar with the situation in the Territories-two very decided and discernible bodies of opinion have arisen. On the one hand, there are the conservationists and the environmentalists who want the park boundaries not only to remain as described in this bill, but to be extended still further. On the other hand, there are those who insist just as strongly that the boundaries are too wide and that within the vast area they enclose, potential exists for mineral development which should not be frozen by the action the minister is taking.
The question could easily be solved had the government followed the suggestion which has repeatedly been made to it, namely, that a resources inventory be taken within the boundaries of the land proposed as a national park. The committee will be hearing these opinions when it goes to the Yukon on December 10. It will be hearing opinions from the Yukon Conservation Society, the Yukon Resource Council, the Yukon Chamber of Mines, the British Columbia and Yukon Chamber of Mines and many other interested individuals and organizations. These opinions will reflect both sides of the question. I see the minister present in the chamber, though not in his place. I know he will be most interested to hear what the committee has to say when it reports to the House.
There is another point I wish to mention. The minister- and 1 do not say this in a denigrating manner-came to the House after I did and he has made one or two statements, both here and in committee, which left the inference that I had in the past been opposed to the establishment of national parks in the Yukon and in the north generally and that I was now coming round to his way of thinking, particularly since the introduction of the bill before us. Nothing could be farther from the truth. If he is fair, after looking at past Hansards he will admit my position has been consistent throughout the 16 years I have sat here, namely that national parks are a requirement in this part of Canada as much as they are in the south. But for heaven's sake the logical approach should surely be to examine inventory resources and hold a public inquiry or hearing before their establishment.
November 26, 1973

This refuge was sought when I was saying to the government, of which the present minister was a member of the treasury benches, that there was no need to stall. I said the government could set up its national park in the Yukon now and that it did not have to wait. The minister's reply, and that of some of his officials was: "Well, we can't very well do that because there are now provisions in the Yukon Quartz Mining Act and in the Yukon Placer Mining Act which would permit mining activities to occur within park boundaries, because they, too, are federal statutes". And indeed they are.
I notice that in clause 11 of the bill the minister has very easily overcome the difficulty, as was suggested to him and his officials in committee, by inserting a subclause that would make the act establishing a park in the north operable notwithstanding any other act of parliament. This is in fact the recurring theme in clause 11. Subclause (2) states that the Governor in Council, which is the cabinet that is going to act on the recommendation of the minister, may after consultation with the council of the Yukon territory or the council of the Northwest Territories, as the case may be, by proclamation set aside as a national park of Canada, and so on, with publication in the Canada Gazette 90 days beforehand, etc.
Consultation in the sense that this bill contemplates consultation means simply nothing. The minister makes up his mind, and the decision having been taken, consultation is window dressing, at least as that word is used in the bill. The minister shakes his head but I have seen this happen so often with the Indian people. I do not know why he shakes his head. He knows full well that the cabinet comes to decisions, and these decisions are then communicated to the organizations concerned. In this case it would be to the Indian Brotherhood, or the Territorial Council, or what have you, and the government would ask: "What do you think of our decision? Isn't it a great thing?" Then, they listen either to kudos or to condemnation, but it does not change their mind one iota and the decision stands. This window dressing clause which says "after consultation" means nothing.
A few years ago when the minister was still in this portfolio but a little fresher than he is now, amendments came before the House to the Yukon Act and the Northwest Territories Act. They had a rough time in committee, even though the government enjoyed a very much greater majority in committees than it does today. We went through this whole process of consulting with the people in the north before making decisions. The government wrote into the amendments to the Yukon Act and Northwest Territories Act the phrase "after consultation with the councils of the respective territories". It was meaningless. Why cannot the government say the same as in clause 2, namely, that there must be agreement with the councils of both territories? Of what is the government afraid? The last referendum taken in the council of the Yukon showed unanimous support in favour of the establishment of a national park. Is the government afraid it might get a negative response if the people of the north were asked to voice a deciding opinion and to make the establishment of the extension of boundaries conditional upon the consent
National Parks Act
or agreement of the two northern territories, as is the case with the provinces?
What about the consultative process of the government in terms of the energy talks with Alberta? That has been about as effective and as meaningful as the consultation phrase as far as this government is concerned. There was no consultation with the province of Alberta about the energy crisis we are now experiencing. I draw these contrasts to the attention of the House because not too many members have been to the northern territories. Not too many realize that the residents of these areas have the same kind of aspirations as any other Canadians. Not too many of them realize that in the territorial councils, which the minister taunts as having all the powers of a provincial legislature, there is less power than the average municipality has in this country.
The people in the north want to be heard. They want to be a deciding factor in any decisions that are made governing their future. They do not object to setting up a national park in the Yukon, but they do object to the minister making a decision and saying: "Here it is; this is what you get, like it or lump it", without any hearings being held. This is why I welcome the fact that this bill has come before the House at this stage, on the eve of the visit of the standing committee to several of the communities in the Yukon that will be very vitally affected by this bill if it passes in its present form.
Mining interests and resource interests are going to present their views in regard to the boundaries, as are the environmentalists. Some of the problems the minister will have to explain and some of the questions that the committee will be unable to answer when they visit there are these: What is going to happen to the dozens of mining claims that have been staked inside the boundaries proposed in the schedules to this bill? Dozens of mining claims have been staked under the provisions of the Yukon Quartz Mining Act; similarly dozens of claims have been staked and leases obtained under the provisions of the Yukon Placer Mining Act. When the committee goes to the Yukon people will say to the members of the committee: "What is the government going to do with respect to reimbursing us for the dollars and time we have spent developing these claims over the years?"
Then, there are people who hold leases on land used for purposes other than mining which is within the boundaries of the proposed park as set out in this bill. Other citizens hold licences to occupy lands within the boundaries of the park as set out in this bill. This committee is a body set up by parliament which will be inviting representations from people in the Yukon. What are the members of the committee going to say to those people when they ask: "Is the government going to pay us? How much money is the government going to give us? Is it going to expropriate our rights? When are the hearings going to be held?" What are we going to answer in reply to inquiries of this kind, the most natural kind of inquiry by people owning interests within the proposed boundaries?
One matter I have not mentioned and of which I know the minister is aware, is the growing body of resource opinion regarding the hydroelectric potential of the Alsek River. Here, I am told, is a natural drainage area which could be developed into a producer of hydroelectric power

November 26, 1973
National Parks Act
in excess of that which is contemplated by the Aishihik project now under way in the Yukon. This was a project that was not even considered by the department when it made the decision to establish the boundaries of this park. Indeed, I am sure the project has only recently come to the minister's attention.
Members of the committee who visit the Yukon now would hear representations concerning such an approach. Having the view I have of the effectiveness of committees of this House as a whole, it is a little too much to hope that anything a committee does, anything it hears and anything it recommends as a result, would receive any worthwhile or meaningful consideration by the minister or this government. We have seen unanimous recommendations come out of committees, I might add not just with this minority government but in a previous majority situation, which have been sloughed aside by this minister and his Cabinet colleagues. Time after time during this session recommendations have come out of that committee, either unanimously or with a substantial majority, only to be ignored.

speechtext: That is not the only example. We have just witnessed one of the greatest examples of this session in respect of the recommendations of the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, also ignored by the government. Indeed, the minister thinks so much of this committee which passed a recommendation by a substantial majority, he decided to reverse that recommendation and nullify the effect of that committee's work. I ask you what the purpose is of committees. They waste hours, days and weeks of time, as well as hundreds of thousands of dollars in taxpayers' money, in a useless and meaningless exercise, bringing recommendations to the attention of this House which are ignored and shoved aside by an unfeeling government. That is what this government means by the beautiful phrase "after consultation with". I only wish that meant something.

speechtext: I agree with you.

I also agree if it only meant something, but it means nothing. The minister knows it means nothing. If he really believed there should be consultation before coming to decisions, he would sit down with the representatives of the two councils concerned before any decision was made affecting the administration of affairs in the north. The minister cannot truthfully say he does that. I am sure the minister sincerely wants to do a good job. He may even think he has achieved some success, and perhaps he is now thinking that if he can bring the James Bay situation out of the fire he will get a new portfolio that is a little less onerous but which provides a little more challenge.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: NATIONAL PARKS ACT

speechtext: There is none better than this one.

subtopic: NATIONAL PARKS ACT

subtopic: NATIONAL PARKS ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT DELINEATING GOVERNMENT'S POWER IN DISPOSING OF PUBLIC LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate as the matter of national parks is of such concern to the province of Saskatchewan. That province has at this time one national park, Prince Albert National Park. Since the early 1960's we have heard a number of proposals relating to a park in southern Saskatchewan to be called the Grassland National Park. This proposal has caused a great deal of confusion and a great deal of concern on the part of the farming and ranching people in that area of southern Saskatchewan. This concern relates to the implications of the establishment of a park in that area for cattle and farming generally. It has also caused concern to many of the so-called nationalists in southern Saskatchewan who for years have been concerned about the grassland areas around Kildeer and Val Marie. They are concerned about the possible destruction of this natural grassland area by the influx of tourists.
In the short time at my disposal, I should like to make several suggestions to the minister and his colleague, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson). Let me make several positive proposals in respect of what might be done to develop a national park in the area without disturbing the lifestyle of the people who have lived there for generations. Mr. Speaker, when the Parliamentary Secretary addressed the House on the second reading of this bill, he made the following statement which I wish to pursue at this time. He stated;
National Parks Act
In its broad concept, clause 2 provides a procedural simplification for dealing with park boundary adjustments. Let me assure you, however, that clause 2 does not authorize any deletions, however small, from parks. I should also like to emphasize that no new park can be established without the approval of Parliament.
I believe it to be absolutely fundamental that should this government or any government, be it Liberal, Conservative, New Democratic or Social Credit, on a federal level suggest the establishment of a new park within the Dominion of Canada it ought to be the right of any member of this House to stand up and speak up on the bill relating to the establishment of a park in his area. I am pleased to see, and I want to spell this out clearly for my constituents, that this legislation does not allow for the establishment of any park without parliamentary authority. Should any government present that kind of legislation, I will endeavour to stop such a bill with all the power I possess. It should be a fundamental rule that members have a right to express their opinion in respect of the establishment of any park, whether it is the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) or my colleague the hon. member for the Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth) or indeed members from southern Saskatchewan, where a proposed grassland national park has been mentioned on several occasions.
What are some of the historical developments related to the federal government's proposed grassland national park? Well, historically the events related to the establishment of the grassland national park began back at least in 1966. In 1966, under the Liberal Government of Saskatchewan, there was a suggestion to the federal government that that province was prepared to enter into the necessary land negotiations in order to establish the national park. In other words, the province was prepared to move in the direction of negotiating with the local farmers and ranchers in respect of the establishment of the grassland national park. This caused a great deal of concern to the people of southern Saskatchewan.
In 1967, the boundary proposed in the report prepared by the National Parks Service reduced the number of square miles for such a park from 640 square miles to 360 square miles. In 1967, the Deputy Premier of the province of Saskatchewan, Mr. Davey Steuart, advised the federal government that, because of the ranching industry and the wildlife involved, there would be $2 million needed for land acquisition. Because of the cost involved in respect of such a park, Saskatchewan at that point in time was opposed to any further consideration of a grassland national park in Saskatchewan. However, in 1968 an economic impact study was undertaken in respect of this national park. It indicated that the benefits exceeded the cost. It was called the Kaplan report. For the minister's sake, I wish to deal with it in order to show that this report, which was put out by a group out of Montreal, was the most outrageous piece of nonsense that has ever been written under the guise of an economic impact study. This report probably did more to stop the development of any proposed park in that area than any other document that was prepared.
In 1969, the Premier of Saskatchewan, at that time Mr. Thatcher, advised that the province would be prepared to reopen discussions if the following points were met: min-

November 26, 1973
Energy Resources Policy
eral rights remain with Saskatchewan; 20-year phasing out for grazing-in other words the farmers and ranchers in the area were to have no future-and federal financial assistance in respect of land acquisition. From 1969 to 1970, negotiations and discussions continued between the two levels of Liberal government. In 1971, a meeting was held in Saskatchewan between the ranchers and the Minister of National Resources of the province to update the ranchers on where matters stood at that time. This meeting was held under the auspices of the new NDP government. In October 1971 the Minister of Mineral Resources of the province of Saskatchewan advised that there had been a change in policy, and that the government did not have the positive attitude towards the development of this park based on the proposals made in the Kaplan report as did the previous government.
In October 1971, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) suggested there be a meeting of federal and provincial officials to carry out the following proposals: identify a core area for each of the two-park components; minimize interruption of ranching and interruption of grazing which might be discontinued; identify outer boundaries of the ultimate park to be realized over a period of time with ranching to continue on the basis of the life tenancy of those ranchers not wishing to sell. It was suggested that if a park were established in the 360 square mile area, then the proposed legislation now before us would give the government the power through Order in Council to extend the boundaries without bringing the matter before parliament. This could have a detrimental effect on the area of southern Saskatchewan where the park is proposed.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MEASURES TO CONSERVE SUPPLY

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MEASURES TO CONSERVE SUPPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in describing Canada's crude oil and products supply situation to this House on November 1, I said that the exact magnitude of the possible oil import curtailment which we might face was uncertain. Stock levels were in delicate balance across the country, with the possible exception of residual fuel oil in British Columbia. Any curtailment would pose problems of supplying some regions of the country and, therefore, I announced the steps the government was then taking to

assess our ability to meet, and to lay plans for dealing with, any shortfalls.
While there are still some uncertainties with respect to the depth of shortfalls we shall suffer, we have, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced on Thursday evening, decided that the facts now warrant embarking upon a voluntary program of energy conservation immediately to be followed by a program of mandatory allocations to be in place early in the new year.
Eastern Canada is totally dependent on imported crude oil and products. British Columbia has historically relied upon some importation of heating oil and residual fuel from the United States. The Arab nations have, until recently provided eastern Canada with 30 per cent of its crude oil supplies. This has amounted to about 300,000 barrels per day. The direct impact of Arab production cutbacks of 25 per cent would, therefore, be 75,000 barrels a day or about 7.5 per cent of our needs in eastern Canada. The cutbacks of 25 per cent of Arab production, however, represent a fall of 20 per cent in total world supply. Canada will have to share, not only in the direct cutback from Arab sources but in the general world shortfall. We may, therefore, suffer a loss, if world shortfalls are shared equally, of up to 200,000 barrels a day. Further, the Arab states have stated their intention of further reductions at the rate of 5 per cent per month from December. Our ultimate shortfall will clearly depend on the speed with which Middle East problems are resolved, but could be in excess of 20 per cent or over 200,000 barrels a day. While it is true, I have said, that our stock positions were adequate and, indeed, held up to 45 days supply of oil products in inventory, even if the Arab nations resumed full production tomorrow at pre-war levels, it is the government's judgment that the situation warrants the actions which I am announcing tonight.
Before describing the nature of the voluntary and mandatory programs, I would like to list the actions we have been taking, some of which have been announced in this House and some of which were alluded to by the Prime Minister both to ease and manage supply shortfalls.
On November 1, I announced the formation of the technical advisory committee on petroleum supply and demand under the chairmanship of the National Energy Board. This committee has been meeting weekly to examine supply and demand slates, to determine stock trends and to provide advice to the government with respect to the over-all supply situation. First, we have sought out and purchased, on government account, supplies of products in world markets. Second, shipments of western Canadian crude oil by Seaway from Sarnia to Montreal, which averaged 17,000 barrels a day in September, will average close to 100,000 barrels a day in November, and will continue at this rate until the Seaway closes. Third, we are organizing and co-ordinating a substantial movement of crude oil and products by rail and truck following the closing of the Seaway. Fourth, we are organizing the movement in excess of 50,000 barrels a day of western crude via the Trans Mountain Pipe Line to Vancouver and via ship through the Panama Canal to Montreal. Sixth, re-arrangements have been made in Trans-Northern product pipeline flows to augment product supplies in eastern
November 26, 1973

Ontario. Capacity will be available for the movement of about one third of the heating oil requirements of the Ottawa area.
Despite these arrangements, we cannot guarantee that the oil that has been and will be lost in the Ontario, Quebec and Atlantic markets can be replaced. The impact of these shortages, particularly of heating oil, will begin to be felt immediately but will be particularly severe in late winter and early spring. I should also note that while we may not experience any immediate shortage of gasoline, the loss of crude oil, together with refiners' efforts to maximize the production of heating oil from available crude are both occurring in a period when stocks of gasoline would normally be refurbished. In the spring, this failure to replenish stocks may be felt in inadequate gasoline supplies.
At the same time that a shortage of international petroleum supplies has been developing, there has been a sharp increase in the price of crude oil coming to Canada from overseas. In his statement to the House of September 4, the Prime Minister indicated that eastern refiners would be permitted to pass on to consumers increased costs resulting from increase in international prices. I have been advised that the costs experienced by eastern refiners have increased again this month, and I have therefore acceded to requests for increases in product prices in that part of the market to be effective December 1. Increased costs vary from refiner to refiner but the average increase is anticipated to be between four cents and five cents a gallon for motor gasoline.
I would like to make one further observation before describing the program of voluntary conservation in which I would urge all Canadians to engage. Eastern Canada and, to a lesser extent, British Columbia, will feel the shortages most. We do not anticipate any shortage in the prairies, but Ontario will feel the effects of our efforts to distribute product supplies equitably. While the mandatory allocation program which I am announcing will deal only in those allocations and those areas where necessary and practical, I am urging all Canadians to embrace the program of voluntary restraint. Oil conserved in the Prairies, for instance, even if it may be transported to other regions only with some difficulty, may yet provide us some needed options in meeting our difficulties.
I would now like to talk about the voluntary program we propose. In my statement of November 1, I concluded by requesting Canadian consumers, municipalities, heavy industry and provincial governments to study means of reducing consumption of energy on a voluntary basis. Since that time, I have received numerous letters from industry indicating the measures they were implementing or planning to implement in order to increase the energy efficiency of their operations. Many provincial and municipal governments have already undertaken voluntary conservation measures, and indeed some governments and industries have gone further than this and launched campaigns to heighten individual awareness of the ways by which energy can be conserved and the savings that can result from voluntary co-operation. I am deeply appreciative of these actions.
Tonight I would like to detail for you some of the measures that the federal government is introducing to
Energy Resources Policy
reduce its own energy consumption, and to speak more specifically about some of the ways in which other Canadians can voluntarily reduce their consumption of energy.
To heat its buildings, the federal government uses about 2 per cent of all the heating oil used in Canada. As a government, we are taking steps to reduce our fuel oil requirements. The Department of National Defence has already undertaken a program designed to achieve substantial cutbacks in fuel requirements, both at home and abroad.
The Department of Public Works has developed a detailed set of guidelines which it will apply to the buildings it administers, and these guidelines will be applied to other federal properties as well, with appropriate modifications in special circumstances. The guidelines recommend that, depending on the nature and the size of building, temperatures be maintained at a maximum of 68 degrees to 70 degrees between 8 a.m. and 5 p.m. on weekdays and 63 degrees to 65 degrees between 6 p.m. and 5 a.m. on weekdays. These lower temperature settings would also prevail on weekends and holidays. As well, the guidelines include detailed suggestions to improve the operating efficiency of heating plants, and to reduce ventilation. At the end of my statement I should like to table a copy of these guidelines.
I should like to stress that these guidelines have been prepared in such a way that they will provide the maximum possible saving with the least amount of discomfort. Indeed, I suspect that many people will find their working conditions more comfortable. We expect that, on average, the actions we propose to take will result in a reduction in federal fuel oil requirements of 18 per cent. Action has already been taken to implement these guidelines and to support them with a co-ordinated reporting and monitoring system.
The savings that we expect in the federal government's own consumption of petroleum are large in percentage terms, but it must be remembered that the federal government's share in total petroleum consumption is fairly small. If we are to significantly reduce the impacts of the foreseen shortages by voluntary measures-as I believe every Canadian wishes to do-then we will require the help of all Canadians.
I am pleased to announce that I met with the energy ministers of the provinces last Friday and believe I have their co-operation in extending the federal guidelines to their own properties to the fullest extent possible.
Tonight, I would strongly urge commercial and industrial enterprises to examine the guidelines set by the Department of Public Works for temperature and ventilation control and to implement them, with modification where necessary, as soon as possible. I would like to stress again that the adoption of these guidelines will result in a minimal loss of comfort and may, in some cases, increase comfort. I know that many of us have experienced overly warm stores when shopping and this is particularly true in the pre-Christmas season when stores are very congested and customers warmly dressed. I would anticipate that reducing temperatures in these circumstances will increase the comfort of the customer, while not seriously inconveniencing sales personnel.
8140

November 26, 1973
Energy Resources Policy
While I am appealing to commercial and industrial users of energy, I would like to make one further point. Industry is expected to observe the guidelines on comfort heating and to improve its efficiency wherever possible in the use of process energy. However, in anticipation of the serious implications which a reduction in industrial process energy could have on the economy as a whole, more particularly in terms of output and employment, industry is not being asked to reduce manufacturing output under this voluntary program.
Industrial and commercial users use almost 25 per cent of total heating oil in Canada, and if significant savings can result in these sectors, we will move a long way toward reducing the shortages that face us. However, Mr. Speaker, the largest single use of heating oil in Canada is for residential heating, and the success of any voluntary conservation program must ultimately rely on the co-operation of individual Canadians in reducing their own space heating requirements.
In the case of large buildings accommodating many people, maximum temperature settings are constrained by the diverse requirements of the many people using a building. Individuals in their residences are freer to adjust temperatures to their own preferences. I would urge that as a minimum individuals maintain temperatures no higher than 68-70 degrees during the day, and about 5 degrees lower at night or when the dwelling is unoccupied. At the same time, I hope that across the country we might achieve average temperature reductions of 5-7 degrees in residences.
I want to emphasize, too, to the Canadian consumer, that saving fuel is saving money. Estimates of savings vary, and depend on such factors as the heat retention capabilities of the building and furnace efficiency. To achieve maximum possible savings, I would again like to table a standard check list of the important steps that can be taken, and I would request each Canadian who is in any way responsible for space heating to put them into practice as soon as possible. It is generally agreed that for each degree drop in temperature fuel savings of 2 per cent to 3 per cent are likely to be achieved. If the target I have set tonight, a 5-7 degree drop in average temperatures, can be attained, Canadian consumers can realize fuel savings of 10 per cent to 15 per cent. There are many different ways of expressing savings of this magnitude.
One way is to tell you that over this winter it can amount to as much as 375 million gallons of heating oil, but I expect that most of you would not find that terribly meaningful. A better measure is perhaps to point out that in dollar terms this saving would amount to about $125 million. But perhaps the most meaningful information I can give you is to put it on an individual basis. An average Canadian household, achieving the targets set tonight, might reduce its winter fuel bill by some $35 to $50, and the oil saved might provide an extra three to four weeks of petroleum supply at the end of the winter season when we expect the impact of the shortages to be most severe.
Next to space heating, the second major area of energy conservation relates to motor gasoline. I have already referred to the gasoline supply position that confronts us
[Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale).J
this winter, and next spring and summer. At the same time you are all aware, from stories in the press, of what the response to gasoline shortage has been in the United States and some European countries.
We have discussed with the provinces the considerations involved in a mandatory reduction of highway speed limits. Such an action would involve considerable expense for provincial governments and we have concluded that it would not, at the moment, be justified. The question of curtailing driving on certain days or at certain times is a difficult one. On balance it seems to us more equitable, if shortages turn out to be critical enough to warrant it, to ration gasoline and let each motorist determine his own driving times, rather than arbitrarily to impose bans on driving which might fall unequally on some people.
The necessity to reconsider these decisions and to impose legislative restrictions on motor vehicle use will depend on the success of voluntary actions to conserve gasoline. It has been estimated that a reduction in speed from 70 mph to 50 mph will result in a gasoline saving between 20 per cent and 40 per cent. Although no legislation is being sought at this point I would urge Canadians, in the strongest possible terms, voluntarily to reduce highway driving speeds to 50 mph. As well, I would again like to table at the end of this statement a standard check list of some of the more important conservation measures motorists can take.
I also want to note that I am not tonight making any specific requests of the transportation sector of the economy. We would not at this time like to see any interruption or serious slowdown in the flow of goods. At the same time we believe these goods should be moved in the most energy efficient manner that is economically feasible, and I would ask the transportation industry to examine its use of energy and to make cutbacks where possible.
Government is initiating steps to ensure that the voluntary guidelines I have proposed will be applied to official vehicles, subject to operational limitations. In addition, actions have been undertaken by the Ministry of Transport to ensure that fuel is used efficiently in commercial air flights, and to assess the saving potential of increased railroad operations in urban areas in an attempt to reduce commuter traffic on the road.
Before leaving this subject I want to speak specifically about car pools, since they are potentially a tremendous source of savings. Calculations suggest that the formation of a four-man car pool and the elimination of three cars driving five miles to a work site could save two gallons of gasoline per day, 40 gallons of gasoline per month, and $6 per person per month. Between now and next summer the saving from one such car pool could be 240 gallons of gasoline and $40 per person for fuel alone. These savings are considerable and tonight I am urging employers, including all levels of government, to take whatever steps they can to assist the formation of car pools. Such actions might range from co-ordinating and organizing car pools, to giving parking spaces on a preferential basis and, if necessary, to examine the possibility of adjusting working hours and shifts. It has been estimated that the conscientious pursuit of conservation measures can yield savings in motor gasoline of anywhere from 15 per cent to 25 per cent over the next year. A 20 per cent saving would result
November 26, 1973

in a saving to the nation of up to 3.75 million gallons of gasoline per day, and an annual saving to the average motorist of as much as $100.
I would like now to say a few words about electric power. In almost every household there are a number of appliances that are major consumers of electricity. In many homes electricity provides space heating as well as hot water. There is no question in my mind that in the longer run we must learn to use our energy resources, all of our energy resources, wisely and efficiently. In the context of the immediate dislocations facing us, however, the conservation of electricity poses special problems. In many parts of Canada, particularly in eastern Canada, electricity is generated by burning petroleum products. In these areas it is essential that conservation measures be actively pursued. In other regions of Canada where the generation of electricity does not depend on petroleum, supply appears to be more than adequate. In these areas it may appear to make sense to use electricity to economize on petroleum products, by such measures as using space heaters in homes. In fact, such actions might seriously strain the capacity of the system and result in service interruptions.
Because the situation is so complex, and because the large and inter-related power networks in Canada make it difficult for the average Canadian to know what the source of his electricity is, I have asked the Energy Minister of the provinces, through their electric utilities, to develop information programs to advise the Canadian consumer on what actions would be appropriate this winter in their regions. I would hope that in this process the utilities would bear in mind substitutions that might be implemented. For example, I am mindful of the security reasons for much of the commercial lighting we see at night. Nevertheless, if commercial lighting requirements would be kept to the minimum necessary, it might, where advisable, be possible for consumers to make more use of electrical space heaters and electric blankets without seriously straining the capacity of the electrical system.
One of the colourful aspects of the Canadian scene at this time of year is the outdoor lighting of homes and commercial establishments to mark the Christmas season. At the risk of being designated as "The Grich who stole Christmas," I would ask individual Canadians, and especially businessmen, to act with restraint this year. If full use of such lighting could be confined to the several days surrounding the festival, significant savings could be achieved.
The measures we are asking the Canadian people to adopt tonight are the result of an intensive evaluation process in which we have tried to isolate the most significant and least disruptive sources of energy saving. I want to emphasize that there are several possible measures that we are not asking for at this time. These include daylight saving time, legislated speed limit reductions, curtailment of Sunday driving, and some measures that other countries have adopted or are considering. Some of these we have avoided because the energy savings would not be that great; others because the potential gains, in our opinion, would be outweighed by the disruptions that would result in the lives of many Canadians.
Energy Resources Policy
I would be wrong, however, to conclude that because we have stopped short of what other countries have done the situation in Canada is not serious. It is indeed serious. It is important, in any serious situation, to maintain a sense of balance, to keep matters in a proper perspective. We hope that we can meet the challenge that faces us without imposing major hardships on any Canadian. But to succeed we must have the full support of all Canadians.
I wish I could give this House the assurance that, given our assessment of the oil supply situation, the saving which will flow from the voluntary conservation program would be sufficient to make a program of mandatory allocations at the wholesale level unnecessary. I can assure the House and all Canadians that a faithful pursuit of the conservation practices I have urged will substantially reduce both the magnitude and duration of the short fall we shall experience. Unfortunately, both our assessment of the probable degree of shortage and the growing inequities which begin to appear in any distribution system when products are in short supply, has convinced us that a mandatory program will be necessary.
I shall be introducing legislation to support the creation of mandatory authority and shall have an opportunity on that occasion to describe more fully the government's intent. I wish only to indicate tonight the major features of this legislation.
First, under the legislation, an Energy Supplies Allocation Board, at the direction and with the approval of the Governor in Council, will have the authority to make allocation directives to ensure equitable distribution of all petroleum products to wholesalers. The legislation will permit the Governor in Council to extend the board's authority to other energy products when and if this might be deemed necessary. Wholesalers will be expected to allocate products equitably to their customers, subject to priorities in allocation to be determined by the government.
Second, in establishing these priorities it will be the government's intention to strike an appropriate balance between the physical comfort and economic health of Canadians. The board will be composed of five people. Two will be representatives of provinces, one of consuming and one of producing provinces. One will represent industry and there will be two federal representatives, one of whom will be primarily concerned to represent the interests of Canadians as consumers.
Third, the board, upon its creation, will assume the direction of the government's efforts and will be responsible for completing the planning for the management of the allocation program as well as assuming the responsibility for the co-ordination of all voluntary efforts.
I have referred earlier to the possibility of gasoline rationing. I wish to emphasize that the mandatory allocation program I have described will not, at the present time, include rationing. The Energy Supplies Allocation Board will have the authority under the act to develop and implement rationing schemes that will apply at all levels including the retail level. The government will request the implementation of such rationing schemes only if the severity of shortages would appear to warrant it.
26695-3i

November 26, 1973
Energy Resources Policy
Finally, I would remind the House that the programs which I have described tonight are designed to deal with shortages brought about by cutbacks in Arab production and therefore, in world supplies. There will be a critical need for these programs until such time as, and only until such time as, world supplies return to normal levels and inventories are replenished. In the meantime, given Canada's relative wealth of energy resources, the government is taking and will continue to take every measure to reduce our vulnerability to foreign supply interruption.
I would suggest, however, that the voluntary conservation measures which I have urged tonight will not only help to alleviate our immediate problems, but have longer run application. We may, in retrospect, look upon the winter of 1973 as the time when each of us became conscious of what has been called the conservation ethic and the understanding that by a rearrangement of priorities and outlook, our life styles would not suffer any critical damage, but might, on the other hand, be substantially enhanced.
Mr. Speaker, I have the three lists, namely, Conservation of Energy in Federal Buildings, Conservation of Energy in the Home and Conservation of Energy in the use of Motor Vehicles. I should like now to table these and I would ask, if the House would give its consent in order that they be distributed, that they might be made an appendix to today's Hansard.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my comments in reply to the minister this evening must be, first of all, on the shocking revelation that the shortage we expected just a few weeks ago of
75,000	barrels a day or thereabouts as being equivalent to our share of the Arab cutback, now turns out to be 200,000 barrels a day. Even being more generous with the figures and allowing for 30 per cent of the 300,000 barrels a day we import from the Middle East, the maximum reduction we should have had to endure was 90,000 barrels a day. We could have looked after that with an all-out effort in this country. Now, we are given the information that we have to find and make up for two-thirds of the total amount of oil imported from the Middle East. I think a lot of questions have to be asked on this point, Mr. Speaker. Where did the 125,000 barrels a day shortage come from? Was it some concession that was made months ago with OECD that not only do we share our own shortages but some of the others as well. These are questions that I think the minister will have to answer, and I hope he stays in the House for the full 20 minute question period to answer them.
Mr. Speaker, I have a few words to say about the voluntary part of the program. There is not much challenge to Canadians in this-no Churchillian phrases here. In fact, if the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. 
Diefenbaker) were in my place he would probably be describing the old-fashioned custom of his day of "bundling" which the minister and I are too young to appreciate.
I do not want to go through a long list of nitpicking suggestions that could be added to the program of voluntary proposals, Mr. Speaker, but in all seriousness I would suggest to the minister and to the government that they not forget the little proposal I made some weeks ago of having the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) immediately state that he would like to give the same sort of reduction and accelerated depreciation to fuel storage units in small towns in eastern Canada, as has been given to large companies. The shortage is going to be with us for some time and an announcement of this type could encourage some of these people to build up storage of heating oil in the summertime when it is not being used so that they would not have to reply on supplies from the big storage facilities in the cities during the winter.
Many years people all over the world have been putting forward ideas for getting more gasoline mileage from their motor vehicles by improving carburetion and so forth, but we have no way of knowing what happens to these ideas. The same thing happens with regard to furnaces and insulation in our homes. I know that there is more information over at the National Research Council on insulation than 90 per cent of the people of Canada know about. We have this practice in Canada of putting our research on the library shelves.
I should like to direct some remarks now to the question of the mandatory program. In answer to questions from the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) a few weeks ago, the minister flatly stated at page 7547 of Hansard for Nov. 5:
A mandatory program is now under preparation but it is not expected to be required.
That was 2Vi weeks ago, Mr. Speaker. I should like the minister to listen to his reply when the Leader of the Opposition asked if this was based on consultation. As recorded at page 7548 of Hansard, the minister said:
I would point out to the Leader of the Opposition, who has had his mouth open through most of my speech rather than his ears, that we are talking about a program which we do not expect will come into existence-
I ask all members of the House and all members of the Canadian public-whose eyes should be opened, whose ears should be opened and whose mouth should be shut?

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MEASURES TO CONSERVE SUPPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MEASURES TO CONSERVE SUPPLY
speechtext:
This government has consistently refused to face up to the possibility of supply shortages from the Middle East. I pointed out to the minister previously in this House that he can go back to questions asked in the Standing Committee on Energy, Mines and Resources, and he can go back to questions asked in this House by members of this party and members of the New Democratic Party about the Montreal pipeline. He can find all sorts of questions about getting supplies from Venezuela, Nigeria and all the rest of it. Always the minister replied that these will not be necessary; there will be lots of supply. At the end of my
November 26, 1973

remarks I will ask for permission to table a list of these questions and answers for the record, so that it will be in Hansard and the minister can easily find it in the future.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MEASURES TO CONSERVE SUPPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MEASURES TO CONSERVE SUPPLY
speechtext:
I mentioned the Montreal pipeline. I hope no one in this House believes for a moment that all we have to do is get through this winter. Montreal is in serious trouble. All of eastern Canada is in serious trouble, and will be for many years to come. On September 4, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) mentioned the decision to build the Montreal pipeline. It is now 2>/2 months later, November 26, and still there has been no action. We have the confusion raised by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) who pointed out there was not any steel to build a pipeline this year or next.
I suggest that the position taken by Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition is good. In 1961 this party issued a national oil policy which at that time was the right policy for Canada. It saved the western oil industry and gave Canada selfsufficiency today which has saved us from the fate our neighbours to the south are facing.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MEASURES TO CONSERVE SUPPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MEASURES TO CONSERVE SUPPLY
speechtext: In 1969, two years after the Arab-Israeli outbreak, our party met in conference at Niagara Falls. We put forward official resolutions of the party calling for a Montreal pipeline to transport 200,000 to 400,000 barrels a day to make sure people would not be cold in the winter. There was no reaction from the government until September 4, 1973. Thers was no reaction of a positive source from the media. All they have said is that westerners are trying to provide us with more oil in the east. I ask this simple question of all members of the House: Where was the Liberal Party when Montreal and Eastern Canada was endangered? We know where they were: they were interested in every other thing but the economics of this country.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MEASURES TO CONSERVE SUPPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MEASURES TO CONSERVE SUPPLY
speechtext: In 1969 our party asked for a change in the national oil policy of 1961. We still do not have an oil policy from this government. One of the very small parts of that oil policy, although an important part, is the Montreal pipeline. I say to the government, on behalf of this party and, I hope, on behalf of all Canadians: build the pipeline now.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MEASURES TO CONSERVE SUPPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MEASURES TO CONSERVE SUPPLY
speechtext:
My
questions in the committee hearings of January and February were ignored. We had the statement by the Prime Minister on September 4. Two and a half months later, still no action. The government is discussing the financing with a private company, Interprovincial Pipe Line. I say, get out and arrange the finances even if the government itself has to build and pay for it. If the government can allocate power and ration gasoline, it can allocate the steel from our steel plants and we can get the project under
Energy Resources Policy
way. Any government with a sense of urgency would have a pipeline built in 14 months, ready for the fall of 1974. Completion of this Montreal pipeline by 1974 would be timed perfectly for the looping of the Interprovincial Pipe Line west. We would have the capacity flowing through. Why should the people of Montreal and all of eastern Canada have to worry each winter for several years while this government dithers, procrastinates and does everything to pose-arrogant at one time; Uriah Heep the next? I think, Mr. Speaker, that I have said enough to make this country aware that it is about time we had a change of ministers on the government side of the House.
May I have the permission of the House to table this fundamental document.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MEASURES TO CONSERVE SUPPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, both the speech made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to the nation last Thursday night, and the speech made by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) to the House this afternoon, gave the impression of a government which had been taken by surprise in finding this country in the throes of an energy crisis. The fact is that this government has been made aware time and time again that we were heading for the present mess in which this country finds itself.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MEASURES TO CONSERVE SUPPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MEASURES TO CONSERVE SUPPLY
speechtext: The problems the country faces with regard to a shortage of oil is the result of the failure of this government to formulate and implement an oil policy. Canada is now going to be required to eat the bitter fruits of this government's procrastination.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MEASURES TO CONSERVE SUPPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MEASURES TO CONSERVE SUPPLY
speechtext:
One of the reasons we find ourselves in this difficult situation is that we have no delivery system to convey western crude to eastern Canada. Canada is one of the two nations in the world which is self-sufficient in oil and gas supplies, and successive governments have received adequate warning about the vulnerability of our position in the absence of a suitable system for conveying western crude to eastern Canada.

November 26, 1973
Energy Resources Policy
During the period I was associated with the government of Saskatchewan, my colleagues and I joined with the Independent Petroleum Producers Association in urging the Conservative government of that day to build a pipeline from Montreal. Since I came back to the House of Commons in 1962 I have made repeated representations to the government on this matter, to the present Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and to preceding ministers in charge of that department. The Independent Petroleum Producers have come before the government repeatedly, drawing attention to the necessity for making secure the oil supply to eastern Canada.
As late as June 28 last, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources tabled the report on energy. On page 14 of that report we read-I suppose the report is speaking for the government-that the threat to security of supply is not sufficient to warrant building a pipeline to Montreal. Yet within a few weeks the Prime Minister, on September 4, announced that the government was in favour of building such a pipeline.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MEASURES TO CONSERVE SUPPLY
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MEASURES TO CONSERVE SUPPLY
speechtext:
When the Prime Minister talked, as he did the other night on the air, about planning ahead, one wonders where this planning is. We have been promised a national oil policy statement for several years. I know of nothing which has had a longer gestation period than the government's oil policy. They started out to put such a policy together four years ago. We have been promised it year after year. We are still waiting for it. The Prime Minister says now that there will be a national oil conference of first ministers in January. If he is correctly reported in the press, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources says he expects nothing more concrete than a policy-and I quote-"evolving as a reality throughout 1974".
What we have seen as a substitute for an oil policy has been a series of ad hoc decisions responding to a series of crises. When some of us in this party warned the government that oil and gasoline were being sent out of the country because of a shortage in the United States, we were ignored and accused of scaremongering tactics. Finally, the government imposed export controls. We pointed out that rising prices in the United States were enabling the oil companies to realize windfall profits. The government finally woke up to the situation and on September 4 imposed a temporary price freeze and put on an export tax.
In recent months, almost every other day we have asked the minister to tell us which alternative sources of oil it is proposed to utilize in the event some of the OPEC countries, particularly the Arab states, refused to make supplies available to us. These questions were set aside with Pollyanna statements that all was well and there was no need to worry. Now we find ourselves in the position where none of the major decisions has been taken with respect to an oil policy.
The minister has not yet told us what the price structure is to be when the freeze is removed. He has not yet told us whether the government intends to set up a national energy corporation and, if so, what its functions and powers will be. He has not told us how he proposes to

develop, in conjunction with the oil producing provinces, the oil sands and the shale deposits. We still do not know the position the government will take with regard to the development of these last great reservoirs of oil a resource which Canada must develop if we are not to face an even more serious energy crisis in the future.
Let there be no doubt about the reason we face an oil shortage at the present time. It is because the government has failed to produce an oil and gas policy. And there is no immediate prospect of one being produced unless hon. gentlemen opposite decide to move much more quickly than they have done up to now.
I appeal to the Prime Minister not to wait until January to call-

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MEASURES TO CONSERVE SUPPLY
speechtext: An election.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MEASURES TO CONSERVE SUPPLY
speechtext:
-a national energy conference. I see no reason why the first ministers could not meet some time in December. I see no reason why the government could not take an immediate decision with reference to the construction of a pipeline to Montreal so that work could begin next spring and we could look forward to its completion before the end of 1975.
The minister has put forward certain proposals, and I wish to comment on them briefly. He said he would establish an energy supplies allocation board which would be responsible for allocating oil supplies at the wholesale level. There is no doubt such a board will be needed, and that the government will have to intervene to make sure that supplies are allocated to areas where they are most required and to see they are distributed fairly. Members of this party would, of course, have preferred to see some type of marketing mechanism. If the government had taken the advice of the energy report that the minister placed before the cabinet last April, the suggestion made by the department that a national energy corporation be set up, we might not be in the situation in which we find ourselves today.
I hope that when the legislation is brought down, the minister will be prepared to tell us what plans the government has made with respect to allocating oil supplies so as to minimize the amount of unemployment which is bound to arise if industries are not able to get adequate supplies of energy. I hope the minister will also tell us, when the legislation comes down, what provision he intends to make to ensure that the independent wholesalers are able to get supplies.
The minister told us in his statement he will make sure that the wholesalers distribute the oil equitably. But will the allocation board ensure that the oil is distributed equally to the wholesalers? Everyone knows that the independent wholesalers depend on the independent oil companies for their oil and that they only get it when the major companies have a surplus. Many of these independent wholesalers service important sections of the Canadian public. We sbfdl be anxious to secure from the minister an undertaking that the independent wholesalers will be able to get a fair share of the oil so that their customers will not suffer.
I note that the minister has acceded to the request that the price of gasoline in the eastern areas of Canada be
November 26, 1973

raised between four and five cents a gallon. I want to point out that the burden of this increase will fall upon that part of Canada which can least afford to carry it. That is why we in this party have pleaded for a national petroleum corporation which would be the sole purchaser of imported and domestic oil, so as to pool all oil and equalize prices right across Canada.
When the minister brings down his legislation, I hope he will tell us how he proposes to deal with the particular problem faced by the province of British Columbia. In that province all of the refineries are geared to producing gasoline. The practice over the years has been to send Canadian oil which comes through the Trans Mountain Pipe Line, to the United States for refining and they sell back to British Columbia the diesel fuel, the middle distillates and the bunker fuel.
Recently it has become increasingly difficult to secure these petroleum products. In British Columbia they have gasoline running out of their ears, but they are having difficulty getting middle distillates, diesel fuel, home heating oil and bunker fuel. At this very moment, in my constituency, a ship with bunker oil is being unloaded. This oil is for one of the mills and is made from Canadian oil that has been processed in the United States, and they are paying $9 a barrel for this bunker oil. Surely this is a matter the minister will have to look into. Otherwise the people on Vancouver Island in particular will be cold this winter because they will not be able to get adequate supplies of home heating fuel.
I agree with the minister when he says we should try allocation of oil supplies at the wholesale level first before resorting to rationing. It is less cumbersome and administratively much easier. If it becomes necessary, of course, we can then look at the situation with respect to rationing. The other set of proposals that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources made related to an appeal to the Canadian people to impose upon themselves voluntary restraints in the consumption of energy. I have no doubt at all that the Canadian people will respond as they always have to a challenge to work together to solve a problem, because it is in our common interest to do so.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MEASURES TO CONSERVE SUPPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MEASURES TO CONSERVE SUPPLY
speechtext:
While I criticize the government, as I have done repeatedly, for its lack of an oil policy, when we are in the situation in which we find ourselves today it is the duty of every good Canadian to co-operate with the government in trying to reduce discomfort and inconvenience to a minimum. However, the minister is going to have some difficulty telling the people of Ontario, for instance, that they should shut off their Christmas-tree lights when Ontario Hydro has asked for permits from the National Energy Board to increase its export of electricity to the United States by over one-third. What makes the situation even worse, Mr. Speaker, is that while the National Energy Board has approved the application and sent it to the government for ratification, the board in the meantime, I am told, has issued emergency permits. It will be very difficult to tell the Canadian people that they have to
Energy Resources Policy
turn off their lights at the same time as we are increasing our electricity exports by more than one-third.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MEASURES TO CONSERVE SUPPLY
speechtext: What is wrong with selling electricity to the Americans?

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MEASURES TO CONSERVE SUPPLY
speechtext:
If I understood the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) correctly, he asked what was wrong with exporting power. I say that it is somewhat illogical to be increasing exports of power by more than one-third at the same time as you are asking the people of the country to turn down the lights. In addition, the minister recommended that we should take the sofa away from the walls and the windows, and also be might have suggested that when young people sit on the sofa they turn the lights out altogether!
It is also going to be difficult to explain to the people who live west of the Ottawa Valley why they should be curtailing their consumption of oil at the same time as we are exporting more than half of our supplies of oil and gas to the United States. I have never suggested that we should cut off our oil supplies to the United States.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MEASURES TO CONSERVE SUPPLY
speechtext: Ah!

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MEASURES TO CONSERVE SUPPLY
speechtext:
But I want to remind the government that its stated policy is that we should only export oil that is surplus to our needs, and that the first demand upon Canadian resources is the needs of the Canadian people. I would further remind the government that until a few years ago our American friends restricted our exports of oil to the United States to 300,000 barrels a day. Now we are exporting over a million barrels a day. If we had not put on export controls, we would not have any oil left for ourselves.
I conclude by saying that I think much of the minister's statement today, like the statement of the Prime Minister last Thursday night, is an attempt to divert public attention from the fact that the government has procrastinated for so long that it has allowed this country to get into this very unfortunate situation. The minister says that when the Arab-Israeli war is over, we will return to normal. I want to remind him that the OPEC nations, and particularly the Arab states, have made it clear that even when the war is over they do not propose to go beyond the production figures they had prior to that time. I think the day may come when we will thank the Arab states for waking us up to the fact that we must develop a policy by which we can use our own resources for the benefit of the Canadian people; and the sooner we get busy and do that, the better it will be for all concerned.

Mr. Speaker, in this-

(a) Lock windows to achieve a better seal.

c)	Open and close doors only when essential

speechtext: In Levis-

We are not dealing with feed grains but with oil. We shall settle the feed grain problem later on.
Mr. Speaker, if we took the necessary steps there would be no oil shortage presently in Canada. I say: I agree. They say: It is an international matter. It is the same argument as in 1929. I say that the oil question is used to cause an economic crisis in Canada, in the United States and in all western countries. This is what they are leading at. They will speak of energy shortage and what do you think will happen if we follow the government program? The closing of plants, restrictions for the producers and ration coupons. This is what we are threatened with. We already had the ration coupons. We have seen that during World War
II.	When I was first elected in 1946, we had the ration coupons. A family mother with ten children was entitled to ten ration booklets, in addition to hers and her husband's. To carry those booklets you needed a special bag. The ration coupons were not made to fit a stomach needs. No. They were printed and the stomach had to fit the size of the ration coupon. This is what we did during the war.
Did that prevent people from getting sugar? I know people in Val d'Or, a doctor among others, who bought ten pounds of sugar at a time. When the ration coupons were issued he had five 100-pound bags of sugar put aside. We bought butter 50 pounds at a time instead of two pounds. We had everything. It is so true that they had to destroy sugar in the Cuba area because there was too much of it everywhere and in spite of that we had ration coupons. I mentioned this in the restaurant of Parliament. Butter was rationed at home but at the restaurant of Parliament we did not need ration coupons and we could eat one pound of butter at a time. We, the members, were not rationed, so I said to the right hon. Prime Minister of the time: If we are not rationed, then we have no right to ration our constituents. It took three weeks, a month, but ration coupons were abandoned and people could obtain

normal supplies. Oil ration coupons and the oil shortage are nothing but a hoax.
The one objective is to get the Canadian population panicky and telling it to freeze slowly in the name of the international oil crisis. Instead of coming out with ration plans, the Creditistes would develop our natural resources for the benefit of the Canadian population and reveal the abundance of Canadian production. This wealth should be developed by the minister who should stop talking of shortages, stop lying as he has been doing, not himself but through his department's officials.
Mr. Speaker, those were the comments that I wished to make on the oil crisis which is only a blind, because it does not exist in Canada. It would not prevent us from transacting with the United States or any other country. But please, let us be frank with the Canadian people and let us tell them why we are really talking about shortages when there is abundance everywhere.
